objectives: State the role of rebar in reinforced concrete.

slides.title: Concrete: ancient material, modern engineering
slides.body:
**Concrete**: mix of cement + water + fine aggregate (sand) + coarse aggregate (gravel/crushed stone). The most-used building material by volume on Earth.

**Cement chemistry**: Portland cement (1824 patent) is calcium silicates + aluminates. With water, they HYDRATE → strong C-S-H gel.

Properties of cured concrete:
- **Strong in compression**: 20-100 MPa typical. Up to 200+ MPa in ultra-high-performance.
- **Weak in tension**: ~10% of compressive strength. Cracks easily.
- **Brittle**: failure is sudden.
- **Durable**: in proper conditions, lasts centuries (Roman concrete still standing).
- **Mass-producible**: poured into formwork; sets in hours, full strength in 28 days.
- **Embodied carbon**: ~6-8% of global CO₂ emissions (cement production releases CO₂ from limestone calcination + fuel burning).

**Sustainability**: huge effort to reduce concrete's carbon. Strategies:
- **SCMs (Supplementary Cementitious Materials)**: replace cement with fly ash (coal byproduct), slag (steel byproduct), silica fume, calcined clay. Up to 50%+ replacement common.
- **Low-carbon cements**: CO₂-cured (Solidia), magnesium-based, geopolymer.
- **CCS-equipped plants**: capture CO₂ from cement kilns.
- **Performance optimization**: use less concrete via better design + higher strength + topology optimization.

**Concrete mix design**: water/cement ratio (w/c) is the most important parameter. Lower w/c = higher strength. Typical 0.4-0.6.
- High w/c → workable + low strength + porous.
- Low w/c → strong + dense + harder to place.
- Admixtures: plasticizers, retarders, accelerators, air-entrainers (for freeze-thaw).

**Curing**: keep moist + warm for first days. Hydration continues for weeks-months. Premature drying → weak + cracked concrete.

slides.title: Reinforced concrete: rebar's role
slides.body:
Plain concrete cracks under tension. To use concrete in tensile loads (beams, slabs, walls), embed STEEL REINFORCING BARS (rebar).

**Composite action**: concrete carries compression + rebar carries tension. Working together they form a strong + ductile structural element.

**Why this works**:
- Steel-concrete BOND: cement paste sticks to rebar surface. Force transfers between them.
- Similar THERMAL EXPANSION: both ~12e-6/°C. Don't separate under temperature changes.
- Concrete PROTECTS rebar from corrosion + fire (until concrete cover spalls).

**Rebar specifications**:
- **Grade 60** (USA): yield 60 ksi (~414 MPa). Most common.
- **Grade 75, 80, 100**: higher strength for special applications.
- **Rebar sizes**: #3 (3/8") to #18 (2.25") in USA. Metric: 10 mm to 50 mm.
- **Deformed** (ribbed surface for bond) — standard.
- **Stainless rebar**: corrosive environments (marine, deicing salt).
- **Epoxy-coated**: bridges (resist deicing salt corrosion).
- **Galvanized rebar**: less common.
- **GFRP** (glass-fiber reinforced polymer): non-corroding alternative. Lower stiffness but no rust risk. Used in MRI rooms, marine, geotech.

**Reinforced beam design**:
- Place rebar in TENSION zone (bottom of simply-supported beam; top of cantilever; both for continuous beams).
- **Tension steel** ($A_s$): primary reinforcement.
- **Compression steel** ($A_s'$): in highly-loaded members.
- **Shear stirrups**: closed loops perpendicular to span. Resist diagonal tension from shear.
- **Concrete cover**: 25-75 mm typical. Protects rebar + ensures bond.

**Strength design (ACI 318 / Eurocode 2)**:
- Ultimate moment capacity: $\phi M_n = \phi A_s f_y (d - a/2)$
- $\phi = 0.9$ for tension-controlled flexure (resistance factor).
- $a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f_c' b)$ (depth of compressive block).
- $d$ = effective depth (centroid of tension steel from top).
- Design check: $M_u \le \phi M_n$ (factored applied vs factored capacity).

**Modes of failure**:
- **Tension-controlled**: steel yields first, concrete crushes after. DUCTILE + safe. Preferred.
- **Compression-controlled**: concrete crushes first. BRITTLE. Code prevents via min steel ratio.
- **Shear**: diagonal cracks. Prevented by stirrups.

**Cracking**: under service loads, concrete tension cracks open BUT rebar carries the tension. Crack widths controlled by code (≤ 0.4 mm typical) for serviceability + durability.

slides.title: Pre-stressed concrete + durability
slides.body:
**Pre-stressed concrete**: pre-tension the rebar (cables/tendons) BEFORE concrete hardens. Result: concrete is in COMPRESSION at service. Cracks don't open. Stiffer beams, longer spans.

Two methods:
- **Pre-tensioning**: tension steel cables in form before concrete pour. Release after concrete cures. Cables grip concrete via bond. Used in factory-precast (beams, slabs, columns).
- **Post-tensioning**: cast concrete with empty ducts. After cure, thread cables, tension, anchor. Used in cast-in-place slabs + bridges + parking structures.

Advantages:
- Longer spans (50+ m feasible).
- Less cracking → better durability.
- Smaller cross-sections (less concrete + steel).
- Cleaner finished surfaces (no rebar imprints).

**Common applications**:
- Parking garages (long spans, thin slabs).
- Bridges (especially segmental construction).
- Long-span building floors.
- Pressure vessels (water tanks).

**Durability problems**:
- **Carbonation**: CO₂ + cement → carbonates. Lowers pH around rebar → loss of passive layer → corrosion. Slow but inevitable in atmospheric exposure.
- **Chloride attack**: deicing salt, seawater. Chlorides penetrate cover, depassivate rebar. Rebar rusts, expansion cracks concrete (spalling). Major issue for bridges + coastal structures.
- **Sulfate attack**: groundwater sulfates attack cement paste. Use sulfate-resistant cement.
- **Alkali-silica reaction (ASR)**: certain aggregates react with cement alkalis → gel formation → expansion + cracking. Use non-reactive aggregates.
- **Freeze-thaw**: water in pores expands when frozen. Use air-entrained concrete.
- **Fire**: concrete spalls at high temp (~300-500°C). Rebar yields. Important for fire ratings.

**Durability design**: 50-100 year design life. Achieved via:
- Low w/c ratio (dense concrete).
- Adequate cover (40-75 mm in aggressive environments).
- SCMs for reduced permeability.
- Coated rebar / non-corroding (FRP, stainless) in critical exposures.
- Cathodic protection (for existing structures).
- Membranes + sealers (bridge decks).

**Modern concrete**:
- **High-performance concrete**: 70-100+ MPa strength. Used in tall buildings, bridges.
- **Self-consolidating concrete (SCC)**: flows without vibration. Used in congested rebar, architectural finishes.
- **Fiber-reinforced concrete**: steel or synthetic fibers replace some rebar. Used in slabs, tunnel linings.
- **Ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC)**: 200+ MPa. Specialty applications.
- **3D-printed concrete**: emerging. Custom geometries; reduce formwork. Commercial buildings being printed.
- **CO₂-cured + low-carbon**: described above. Active commercialization.

question.question: Compute moment capacity of an RC beam
question.goal: Beam: width $b = 300$ mm, effective depth $d = 500$ mm. Concrete $f'_c = 30$ MPa. Tension steel: 3 × #25 ($A_s = 3 \times 491 = 1473$ mm²). Grade 60 ($f_y = 414$ MPa).

steps.prompt: Compression block depth: $a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f'_c b)$.
Compare to factored applied moment. If applied factored $M_u = 220$ kN·m, beam adequate?

options: Adequate: $\phi M_n = 253 > M_u = 220$. ~15% extra capacity (safety factor in addition to factored loads).

steps.reveal: Adequate. 220 < 253. The beam can resist the design moment with ~15% additional margin. Final check: code-mandated minimum + maximum steel ratios + shear capacity + deflection + durability.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\phi M_n = \phi A_s f_y (d - a/2); \text{ where } a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f'_c b)}$$ Reinforced concrete moment capacity is the fundamental calculation in structural design. Every beam, slab, column requires this analysis. Modern: code calculations are automated in software (Bentley, Tekla, RAM, RISA, SAFE). Hand calc still valuable for sanity check + initial sizing. The formula assumes tension-controlled (ductile) failure; code ensures this via steel-ratio limits.

question.question: Why is reducing concrete's carbon footprint important + how?
options: Cement production releases CO₂ from limestone calcination + fuel; concrete is ~7% of global CO₂. Reduction strategies: SCMs (fly ash, slag, calcined clay), low-carbon cements (CO₂-cured, geopolymer), CCS at plants, design optimization. Each strategy delivers 10-50% CO₂ reduction.
question.explanation:
Concrete = ~7% of global CO₂. Cement (the binder) is the issue: limestone calcination releases CO₂ inherently (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂); fuel burning adds more. Strategies: 1) SCMs replace cement (fly ash from coal plants, slag from steel mills, calcined clay) — up to 50% replacement. 2) Low-carbon cements (CO₂-cured, magnesium-based, geopolymer) — emerging tech. 3) CCS on cement plants. 4) Design optimization (use less concrete via stronger mixes, topology optimization, performance-based design). Industry roadmap to net-zero ~2050.

Big deal: cement is the SINGLE LARGEST industrial CO₂ source after fossil fuels. Decarbonizing concrete is one of the biggest climate challenges + opportunities. Major companies (Holcim, CEMEX, Heidelberg) all have net-zero commitments.

slides.workedSolution: Cement = ~7% global CO₂. Limestone calcination releases CO₂ inherently. Kiln fuel adds more. Solutions: SCMs (replace cement with fly ash, slag, calcined clay) — up to 50% replacement; low-carbon cements (CO₂-cured, geopolymer); CCS at plants; design optimization (less concrete via stronger mixes). Industry committed to net-zero by 2050. Critical decarbonization sector.

question.rubric: Mentions that concrete is strong in compression but weak + brittle in tension; steel is strong + ductile in tension but expensive + corrodes; combining them: concrete carries compression + steel carries tension + steel is protected from corrosion by alkaline concrete; the composite is strong, ductile, affordable, durable. The 19th-century invention of reinforced concrete revolutionized construction; modern engineering refines mix designs + steel grades + analysis methods.
